reasoning:
Here is a research-based synthesis of the effectiveness of generative AI tools (especially large language models, LLMs) for skill development among high/secondary school students, based on peer-reviewed and reputable sources from the past five years. This summary prioritizes studies according to evidentiary strength per the Evidence Ladder and includes direct links to original research.

---
## 1. Types of Skills Targeted

### Academic Skills
- **Literacy & Writing:** LLMs like ChatGPT are used for writing support, reading comprehension, and providing feedback. Automated feedback from LLMs can enhance literacy and writing outcomes, particularly if prompt design and feedback quality are well-managed.
  - Meta-synthesis and implementation studies (Rung 2–3):
    - Kumar et al. (2024). "Taking Responsibility for Meaning and Mattering: An Agential Realist Approach to Generative AI and Literacy." Literacy Research & Practice. [Full text](https://dx.doi.org/10.1002/rrq.570)
    - Tian et al. (2026). "Optimizing Language-Focused Writing Feedback from Large Language Models through Prompt Engineering." [PDF](https://edtechbooks.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/pdfs/2551/25147.pdf)
  - Comparative empirical study (Rung 3):
    - Schmitz & Sonnleitner (2025). LLM-generated vs. human-written reading comprehension passages for assessment. [Full text](http://dx.doi.org/10.1186/s40536-025-00255-w)

- **Critical Thinking and Argumentation:** LLMs are used in structured debate/argumentation tools to enhance reasoning and self-reflection.
  - Quasi-experimental study (Rung 3):
    - Jho & Ha (2024). "Generative AI-Based Evaluation and Feedback System for Argumentation Skills," showing comparable reliability to human expert assessment. [Full text](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1422722)
  - Meta-analysis (Rung 4):
    - "Does Generative Artificial Intelligence Improve Students' Higher-Order Thinking (HOT)?" (2025): Pooled effect size g=0.61 for HOT (including problem-solving, critical thinking, creativity); strongest on problem-solving (g=0.75), followed by critical thinking (g=0.69), moderate effect on creativity (g=0.44). [PMC Open Access](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12734368/)

### Non-Academic Skills
- **Creativity & Communication:** Evidence for substantial gains in creativity is mixed; most studies find moderate improvements, especially for collaborative or prompt-based tasks, but over-reliance may suppress original thinking if not scaffolded.
- **Student Voice & Autonomy:** Qualitative research suggests LLMs can boost student agency, particularly in settings where students co-design prompts or evaluate model outputs.
  - Riser (2025): Teachers report increased student autonomy and voice in AI-enabled classrooms. [Full text](http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/04250494.2025.2491361)

- **Engagement:** Surveys and case studies report increased engagement—especially for students who previously struggled—but this is highly dependent on context and implementation fidelity.
  - Zhou & Hou (2024). Study in EFL settings found that AI use improved behavioral and emotional engagement. [Full text](https://doi.org/10.1111/ejed.12750)

---

## 2. Evaluation Metrics Used

- **Academic Performance:** Exam/test scores, writing quality rubrics, reading comprehension, and argumentation performance.
- **Skill Assessments:** Standardized tests for critical thinking/problem-solving, rubrics for creativity, and content analysis of student work.
- **Feedback/Perceptions:** Structured surveys, interviews, and reflective journals from both students and teachers.
- **Engagement Metrics:** Self-report, attendance, assignment submission, platform log data.

Sample studies that used these methods:
- Tian et al. (2026): Used pre- and post-tests of writing with rubric-based evaluation. [PDF](https://edtechbooks.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/pdfs/2551/25147.pdf)
- Jho & Ha (2024): Compared LLM scoring with expert-human scoring for argumentative writing. [Full text](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1422722)

---

## 3. Contexts Studied (Geography and Equity)

- **Geographic Breadth:** Studies include Japan (LLM in English education), Malta (minority language learning), USA, EU, and multilingual/immigrant populations.
  - Lee & Eronen (2025): Examined LLM integration in Japan’s English curriculum. [Full text](http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s44217-025-00856-1)
  - Zammit (2025): LLM adaptation for Maltese language classrooms. [Full text](http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s10758-025-09861-7)
- **Socio-economic settings:** Both high- and low-resource school contexts are studied. Meta-analytic work shows no systematic disadvantage in outcomes based solely on SES, but access (device/internet) may limit impact in under-resourced settings.
  - Yim & Su (2024): Scoping review on K–12 AI literacy initiatives globally. [PDF](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9.pdf)

- **Classroom vs. Extracurricular:** Most evidence is from classroom-integrated interventions, though some programs report on afterschool or project-based learning. Highest gains are reported in structured curricular integration over 8–16 weeks.

---

## 4. Strength of Evidence (Evidence Ladder)

- **Rung 4 (Experimental/Meta-Analysis):**
  - Meta-analysis of 29 RCT/QED studies: Moderate positive effect on higher-order thinking, strongest for problem-solving and critical thinking (see above). [PMC Open Access](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12734368/)
- **Rung 3 (Quasi-Experimental/Matched Comparison):**
  - Several studies comparing AI feedback/scoring to human-expert assessment (e.g., argumentation, writing) and showing similar or sometimes more timely/effective results.
  - Teacher and student perception studies aligning with skill-gain metrics.
- **Rung 2–1 (Qualitative/Implementation):**
  - Rich qualitative findings on classroom practice, engagement, and perceptions (esp. for minority languages or marginalized groups), but less rigorous evidence of learning outcomes.

---

## 5. Equity and Heterogeneity

- Some studies analyze subgroup results:
    - Project GLIMPSE (US): Focus on multilingual and twice-exceptional students, using AI to reduce equity gaps in gifted/talent identification. [PDF summary](https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/2022/08/S206A220026-The-School-District-of-Osceola-County-Florida.pdf)
    - Jho & Ha (2024): Reliability across scientific/non-scientific contexts and demographics.
- No "universal gains": Outcomes are most positive when LLMs are systematically integrated, with scaffolding and adaptive feedback tailored to students’ self-regulation and motivation.

### Key Risks
- Over-reliance can suppress self-regulation/creativity if students use LLMs only for answer generation.
- Misalignment between model output and classroom standards requires careful oversight.

---

## Direct Links to Key Original Studies

- Meta-Analysis (RCT/QED): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12734368/
- Argumentation Feedback/Assessment: https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1422722
- Literacy & Writing with LLMs: https://edtechbooks.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/pdfs/2551/25147.pdf
- English Education Reform in Japan: http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s44217-025-00856-1
- K–12 AI Global Review: https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s40692-023-00304-9.pdf
- Minority Language Teaching: http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s10758-025-09861-7

---
## Summary Table: Evidence and Key Findings

| Skill Area                  | Evidentiary Level | Effects/Outcomes        | Equity Findings         | Context (Country)             |
|-----------------------------|-------------------|------------------------|------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Critical thinking, HOT      | Rung 4 (Meta/RCT) | g=0.61 (moderate)      | Higher for SRL/motivat.| Cross-national                |
| Problem solving             | Rung 4 (Meta/RCT) | g=0.75 (strong)        | -                      | Cross-national                |
| Creativity                  | Rung 4 (Meta/RCT) | g=0.44 (moderate)      | Sensitive to over-reliance | Cross-national           |
| Literacy and writing        | Rung 3–4          | Positive, contextual   | Some evidence for ELLs, low-SES | U.S., Japan, Malta   |
| Communication, engagement   | Rung 2–3          | Higher engagement      | Variable: higher with interactive practices | U.S., EU, global |
| Gifted/talent identification| Rung 2            | Early trends positive  | Significant equity role   | U.S. (Hispanic/ELL/2e focus) |

---

## Conclusion

- Generative AI/LLMs show moderate-to-strong evidence for enhancing critical thinking, problem-solving, and literacy skills in secondary education when well integrated and scaffolded.
- Gains in creativity and communication are present but depend heavily on instructional method and student agency.
- Teacher and student feedback is generally positive, but also highlight concerns about over-reliance, academic integrity, and alignment with learning goals.
- Rigorous, replicated RCTs/meta-analyses support causal impacts for academic skills; qualitative and quasi-experimental data support implementation/engagement outcomes.
- Equity-promoting potential is evident—especially in multilingual, ELL, or low-resource contexts—if access and scaffolding are in place.

For the most authoritative synthesis, see this meta-analysis: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12734368/
